speechtext: 94th anniversary of confederation

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this Dominion day, the 94th anniversary of founding the nation, before we proceed with consideration of today's business may I invite hon. members to pause and pay tribute to the fathers of confederation whose faith and prophetic insight brought this nation into being?
Federation was a prerequisite to the national development of Canada, and the maintenance of national unity remains the key to its destiny. I know there are some who feel a sense of embarrassment in expressing pride in their nation, perhaps because of the fear that they might be considered old fashioned or parochial. I do not belong to that group. I realize that a warped and twisted nationalism is productive of tyranny and war, but that a healthy loyalty and devotion to one's country constitutes a most fruitful inspiration in life.
While our nation had its beginning in two great races today we can take pride in the fact it is now the debtor to many ethnic groups. Six years from today we shall be observing the centennial of confederation. I think it is timely that on today's Votes and Proceedings notice is given of a resolution to precede a bill respecting observance of the centeimial, to authorize the establishment of a national centennial administration in cooperative form, to plan and prepare projects and programs to be undertaken by the government of Canada in order to mark the centennial, and to provide also for the establishment of a national conference on the centennial which will constitute a forum for consideration by both governmental and non-governmental representatives.
Today in celebrating this day by carrying on our duties as public servants we do our part to help achieve the highest ideals of the fathers who made this nation possible. After the Leader of the Opposition and a representative of the third party have spoken their words regarding this day, I suggest that the house then rise and sing O Canada and God Save the Queen.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposiiion):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am sure there is no one in this house who has any fear or hesitation in expressing his pride in our country in its growth and development in the last 94 years. I am sure we all feel that a healthy nationalism is the foundation of that growth and development. This is our 94th birthday. It reminds us, as the Prime Minister pointed out, that in six years we shall be celebrating our centennial. Our country is growing older in years and I hope in wisdom and maturity as well. This is the day of the year when we assess the past and, if we are wise, in terms of the present and of the future. We can take pride in that past and from it resolve to play our part so as to make the future worthy of it and of those great men whom we honour today who founded and helped to build our nation.
We must then work together, as indeed we are working here in parliament today, on Dominion day, to do our part to make our country great in strength and unity, a unity which is not uniformity or centralization and a strength which is more than gross national production.

Mr. Speaker, being somewhat of an ancient in years I am inclined to think of the past on these occasions. Looking at the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) I recall very vividly that 47 years ago he and I celebrated July 1 in a little village in my constituency known as Nakusp, on the occasion of the opening of the Nakusp-Kaslo railroad. Forty-four years ago today I was in a hospital after being knocked about a bit, and that was the first occasion that I was particularly conscious of my pride in being a Canadian. I suppose it was principally on account of being away from Canada at that time and its associations.
Today the great majority of Canadians will celebrate Dominion day as our national holiday. We trust they all enjoy themselves. However, on behalf of this group I do want to say we are of the opinion that we are not setting a good example in the recognition of this national holiday by parliament sitting today; not because we would not be willing to sit and undertake the business of the country, but we think in the first instance it is a poor example, and in the second instance it is unfair to the staff of parliament. I trust that in future years this matter will receive

U.K. Action in Kuwait serious consideration, so that all Canadians will have the opportunity to celebrate Dominion day.

subsubtopic: KUWAIT-STATEMENT ON ACTION BEING TAKEN BY U.K. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will have heard news reports of the latest developments in Kuwait. This potentially serious situation has arisen as a result of the claim of Iraq that Kuwait forms part of the territory of Iraq. This claim, of course, is contested by the government of Kuwait, which is a sovereign and independent state and which, in order to safeguard its security and independence, has requested assistance from the United Kingdom government under an agreement concluded between the two countries on June 19, the date on which the former treaty of protection ceased to have effect.
Prime Minister Macmillan has been in touch with me and has explained the circumstances in which the United Kingdom government has felt obliged to honour its commitment to the ruler of Kuwait by acceding to his appeal for assistance. He has informed me of the steps which the United Kingdom government is taking, and also that a report on these steps is being made to the United Nations at once. Indeed, the government of the United Kingdom has asked that the security council be convened today. Mr. Macmillan has made it clear that the purpose of the action taken is to discourage any attempt to interfere with the sovereignty and independence of Kuwait.
Early this morning I sent word to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom that in the difficult circumstances of this situation I believed that he could not have done otherwise than respond to the appeal of the ruler, and welcomed the United Kingdom government's
[Mr. Herridge.l

action in reporting to the United Nations the steps which it is taking. I also assured him that our representatives at the United Nations would do their best to be of assistance in any way open to them in that organization.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: KUWAIT-STATEMENT ON ACTION BEING TAKEN BY U.K. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has rightly referred to this situation as a serious one. Indeed, it is a threat to peace. I suggest that the principle upon which action should be based is the principle embodied in the charter of the United Nations. This is more than a principle; it is an obligation on all of us to resist collectively any aggression wherever it may appear. I hope this resistance will not be required because I hope no such aggression will take place.
It is good to hear from the Prime Minister that the matter has been referred to the United Nations, and we on this side certainly support the stand that has been taken by Canada in reply to the message received from the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.

subsubtopic: KUWAIT-STATEMENT ON ACTION BEING TAKEN BY U.K. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The
members of this group are particularly glad and interested to know that the Prime Minister of Canada is being kept informed by the Prime Minister of Great Britain with regard to this serious situation. We appreciate the Prime Minister informing the house of developments at the first opportunity. We are glad to know of Canada's co-operation, concern and interest, and also that the matter has been referred to the United Nations.

subtopic: POPULARITY OF ARTHUR MEIGHEN COMMEMORATIVE STAMP
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Postmaster General. Will the minister inform the house whether there is any truth in a statement that appears in this morning's Montreal Gazette to the effect that the Arthur Meighen commemorative stamp is less popular than are other stamps in that class?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: POPULARITY OF ARTHUR MEIGHEN COMMEMORATIVE STAMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purchase of any commemorative stamp is resisted by a percentage of our patrons. In the past I have referred to them as the dry tongue group, because they find the commemorative stamps usually are larger in size and somewhat more difficult to lick, and they prefer to use the normal queen size stamps. We therefore have some patrons who prefer not to purchase any commemorative stamp that is issued.
I inquired this morning after the newspaper story appeared; that was the first indication I had. In this particular case there is absolutely no evidence whatsoever that this stamp has been less popular than any other commemorative stamp that we have issued. As a matter of fact, those who are expert in the field of aesthetics have generally felt that this particular issue was the best of all the prime minister commemora-tives we have done in so far as design and execution were concerned.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CROP CONDITIONS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Speaker. In view of the welcome report of rain in the prairie provinces, I wonder if the minister could bring us up to date with regard to any recent developments in that region, particularly as to whether there has been any appreciable change in the crop situation having regard to that report. Could the minister tell us, further, whether he has any plans for meetings with provincial ministers to discuss the fodder situation on the prairies?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CROP CONDITIONS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I think everyone in Canada will be pleased to hear that there has been some rain in western Canada in the last 24 hours. These rains were due to a stationary front over most of the northern part of the three prairie provinces. The southern parts of the provinces have not benefited to the same degree. There have been showers, and rainfall between .1 inch and .5 inch have been registered. This will mean that the pastures will be revived to some degree, and brings the hope that the crops can hang on for a few more days during which time further rain may come.
The three agriculture ministers of the prairie provinces and I will be meeting in Winnipeg tomorrow to work out details of a series of programs which we have in mind in case the situation should deteriorate to a disastrous extent.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. For a good number of years the city of Trail has been interested in an urban renewal scheme. At the time the Secretary of State for External Affairs was minister of public works he made it possible for a survey to be made of the whole situation through an appropriation from this department. Since that time the survey has been completed and

Supply-Public Works
the city of Trail has had a committee working on this question. That committee has negotiated with the Canadian Pacific Railway in respect to the removal of a section of track, and has had lengthy negotiations with provincial authorities. Trail is now prepared to proceed and is very anxious to obtain final endorsation of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in respect to this scheme.
To illustrate the concern which exists I should like to quote briefly from the Trail Times of Thursday, May 4, 1961 and specifically from an article appearing therein entitled "Federal Government Studying First Phase of Urban Renewal Scheme". That article reads in part as follows:
First phase of Trail's urban renewal development, that of West Trail, now is in the hands of the federal government, Mayor Leslie Read told the retail section of the Trail chamber of commerce Wednesday night.
"It has been there two weeks," he admitted. "One month is all the time we are going to give them. If there is no word by then we will press the matter."
"To us," said the mayor, "urban renewal means a lot; and $1,100,000 is a lot of money to a city this size."
The article then continues as follows:
In reviewing the history of urban renewal in Trail, Mayor Read told merchants that when he first came into office (1956) track removal problem was one of the major problems confronting the council.
Then the article continues as follows:
Mayor Read said the B.C. government has approved the first phase and agreed to pay 25 per cent of the cost. Trail also pays 25 per cent and the federal government, if it approves the plan, pays 50 per cent.
"We hope the federal government will understand our problem," continued the mayor. "If they reject the plan it means, then, that the onus would be on the provincial government to increase its share of the cost".
I raise this matter at the request of the local people because they are very interested in this problem. I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs is also interested, because he was recently appointed the first freeman of Trail, and I congratulate him on that appointment and honour. I am not quite sure of the rights, responsibilities and privileges granted to freemen of a city in British Columbia, but I looked the matter up with respect to Great Britain and found that in Great Britain it is based on the honourary freedom of boroughs act of 1885, under which there are certain privileges. In some instances the freemen do not pay taxes; in others they are allowed to lead their cows in the city without any interference. In other instances they are responsible for the poor of the district. I am not quite sure what responsibilities the minister has assumed, but I congratulate him and I am sure he is

as interested as any member in this house in this renewal problem in the city of which he has been appointed the first freeman.

speechtext: He is sitting on his keeping them warm.

You see what happens, Mr. Chairman. Hon. members opposite say "Stay in order" and then they make these inane and asinine cat-calls and interjections which are completely out of order and made for the sole purpose of delay.
Mr. Chairman, for the purpose of the record may I say that I made no interjection or cat-call except to ask the hon. member to come to order.

If the hat fits, pull it right down over your ears if you feel like it. The National Housing Act was amended in 1956 to provide that loans may be made to Indians for the purpose of building homes, and reconstructing and bringing homes up to date on Indian reserves, but so far no such loans have been made and I understand that no Indians have applied for loans. Without being derogatory in any way, I think we all agree that generally speaking the standard of homes on Indian reserves is not as high as in communities outside Indian reserves. I think this arises from a variety of reasons, economic, educational and others.
There is great need for an adequate home building program and adequate credit facilities for the Indian people in order that the homes they have at the moment may be

Supply-Public Works
brought up to a higher standard. Even though the National Housing Act was amended in 1956 to provide for the making of such loans to Indians, I think the reason no applications for loans have been made is simple. Indian land cannot be mortgaged. It is land held in trust by the crown for the Indian population and it cannot be mortgaged, attached or foreclosed in any way. I think this is the main reason the provision with respect to loans to Indians under the National Housing Act has had no beneficial effects. Their lands cannot be pledged as security, which is the normal basis for the securing of mortgages for the building of homes so far as other people are concerned.
I realize that this is an extremely complex matter and can be easily misunderstood, but I think what must be explored is the possibility of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation working in conjunction with the Indian affairs branch to develop a system of lending money to band councils on the basis of having the natural resources of the band mortgaged as security for the loans. In this regard I am thinking not of the land itself, which I do not think should be attached in any way, but rather of such things as the timber, oil or minerals on the land. If there was default in repayment these natural resources could be leased, sold or rented, as is now done by Indian bands in many instances, in order to recover the amount of any loan that was in default. In the process of relending the money borrowed under the National Housing Act the band council would be able to take as security from the individual band member that person's per capita share of the band fund and I think also the right to possess the property held by the individual Indian on the reserve in order that the band council might protect the resources of the band.
Unless we can do something of this nature I think the presence in the National Housing Act of a section authorizing loans to Indians will continue in the years to come to be of no use whatsoever, because at the moment there is no way in which Indian lands can be mortgaged. If this field has not already been explored I sincerely hope the minister will explore it fully and completely, to ensure the highest possible standard of homes for Indian people on reserves, and through this means attempt to see that the environmental factors of our Indians with respect to home conditions more closely approximate the environmental factors of those of us who are not Indians.
This would be another way of moving toward equality as between Indians and non-Indians. If investigation and study have already been made with regard to the matter

of loans to Indians, I would appreciate it if the minister would indicate the results of these studies. On the other hand, if nothing definite has been done so far in this regard I am sure it would be a profitable field to explore, and would assist the Indian people immeasurably in increasing their standard of living.

I have always understood that the corporation was given a certain amount of money and that the government as they have done on several occasions, made large additional grants to the corporation with the idea that the money would be placed in a revolving fund for at least the term of the mortgages and that the amount would continue to grow. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:

speechtext: It has been stated-and I am not supporting the validity of the statement, because I am not qualified to do so-that the standards laid down are so strict that they add to the cost of construction, and that perhaps for that reason they may be considered too strict.

One thing which appears to me to be self evident is that the planning which went into the central mortgage and housing development in Elliot Lake was at fault. A terrific expense was imposed on many of the miners in that area in order to do something which

was demanded of them by this act when it was probably not necessary to incur such expense, and not to their advantage to do so. The government knew. The officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation knew. They were more aware than anyone else of the fact that Elliot Lake was a temporary proposition with a very doubtful future. They made this evident in the requirements they imposed in asking the companies to guarantee beyond a very limited period the loans which were made at that time. Even so, even knowing this, standards were set for the building of houses which would probably be advantageous only if more permanent buildings were required. Why should such standards have been set at a time when it appeared1 to the officials of the department that this township was not going to be as permanent as had once been indicated?
Such mistakes are repeated in other areas. We are told that houses are to be built in the city of North Bay in connection with defence requirements. The units to be built by the department are being planned in several locations, and I presume they will be built in accordance with the standards which apply to normal housing. I think it is generally accepted, even by the people who will be living in these houses, that there is not likely to be a 20-year tenancy. The Bomarc missile base in North Bay will not be as permanent as that, in all likelihood. Military minds can probably see what is likely to be the lifetime of that community as it is being planned. I do not believe it is necessary or desirable to have these houses built in accordance with plans which are thought to be desirable when houses are to last for 50 or 60 years. I think much more temporary arrangements could be made, and that these would be satisfactory for the housing of these people.
I should like to know what work the department has done in the matter of planning in so far as the relationship between the cost of acquisition of a site and the cost of the house to be built on it is concerned. It appears to me unreasonable to build a $10,000 or $12,000 house on a piece of land which costs $10,000, for example. The department must have worked out a formula in connection with the relationship between the value of the house and the cost of acquiring the land on which it is built.
Of course this situation is governed to some extent by municipal bylaws. Certain zoning bylaws call for the erection of certain types of house, but the department has no doubt done some work on this question. I am interested to learn what the results have been, and whether there is a formula or relationship between the cost of acquiring the land and the price of building to be built on the land.

In relation to the work which the minister said would be done at North Bay-he referred to projects located in several areas- I understand that the options and planning have already begun in regard to a 200 unit project, and that consideration is being given to the sites required for the remainder of the total of 575 homes. I should like to know what the department's thinking is in regard to fitting this program into the housing program of the municipality, and what advantage or disadvantage there is in keeping the military housing project separate from the municipality. I understand when this course is followed the military project is only connected to the municipality in order to obtain municipal facilities such as sewer and water services. Is there a formula which has been developed in this regard and, if so, what are the advantages?
It seems to me that it would have been advantageous in past years if during the planning of low cost housing projects consideration had been given to including them as part and parcel of the municipality rather than locating them in isolated areas. Such a course, I suggest, would have been advantageous to any urban renewal program carried out at a later date, after the lifetime of those low cost housing units, which was considered at the time they were built to be very limited. Had that course been followed the whole area would have benefited by a total urban renewal program rather than one which concerns only certain streets, areas and zones, and which involves great difficulty because of the fact that the low cost houses have decreased the value of surrounding properties.
I should like to know whether this department has considered this program in those terms, with particular reference to the project at North Bay. I should also like to know why in the planning and development of this and similar projects the same consideration was not given as was given the development of areas such as Elliot Lake and Bancroft, where very high standards were demanded in respect to buildings because the officials of the department were of the opinion that it would be advantageous to do so; and I suggest that is so because of the financing arrangements that were made with the companies involved.

I am sure that the residents of the national capital and all other Canadians who are interested in the national capital development, have noticed with pleasure the progress made up to now in the implementation of the plan.
Since we are at present considering the item relative to the operation and maintenance of parks and parkways, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the staff and all the members of the commission for the excellent work they are doing in this city. We are very proud of our parks and parkways; tourists who visit the national capital never have anything but words of praise for the way the flowers and shrubbery are kept and for the fine condition of the grounds around government buildings.
I therefore commend all members of the commission and all those responsible for the maintenance and lay-out of those parks.

Supply-Public Works
The national capital program provides tor projects to be carried out in the immediate future, and others are long term projects.
I want, at this time, to congratulate the commission for having undertaken the important project of relocating the railway tracks and Union station. That, to my mind, is the key to the master capital plan. It was announced earlier in the press that within four years, Union station would be located about two miles from the parliament buildings. All the railroad tracks across the city will disappear; the level crossings will be eliminated, and new throughways and boulevards will be laid out where those tracks are now.
I read with great pleasure in the papers, about ten days ago, that the commission had decided to run the railways underground in the city. From the Ottawa river the route would go under the Rideau canal to the south of the city via the Carleton university campus. I think that is a sound decision, though it may cost rather more to have those tracks running through a tunnel. From an aesthetic point of view, it will mean a great deal to the capital.
As far as railroad relocation is concerned, I hope that the commission is now considering a similar plan for the city of Hull. We know that in four years from now, when Union station has been moved a few miles away from its present location, the railway on the Quebec side will also have to change its route, because trains will no longer be using the interprovincial bridge. Railway traffic will be concentrated on a single branch line. I hope the commission will proceed in the same way on the Quebec side as on the Ottawa side. I hope consideration will be given to building a tunnel for the railroad tracks west of Montcalm street and beyond Alexandre Tache boulevard. The same might be done on the north side of the city of Hull, towards which much of the traffic will have to be routed when the new bridge is built. At that time, I think it would be very wise to build a tunnel for the railroad tracks across Hull.
May I also say to the house that I am most satisfied with the attitude adopted by the commission in purchasing all the land on the Ottawa side in the green belt surrounding the national capital. Such a step was essential both for sound administration and as a means of rushing in a scientific way the boundaries of the capital area.

I hope the commission will adopt the same policy on the Quebec side and will take immediate steps for the creation of a green belt in that area.

Mr. Chairman, before the one o'clock recess, I made a few brief remarks on the administration of the national capital.
I should now like to discuss a subject of great concern to my constituents and to myself, namely the development of the Gatineau park.
I am sure the majority of hon. members who have visited the park will agree with me that we would feel more comfortable this afternoon in Gatineau park than in this house.
A great many Canadians are on holidays at this time, enjoying the charms and facilities available to them as a result of the development of Gatineau park.
Gatineau park is only partly developed.
The scheme for the development of this park was outlined in 1937. First there was the planning stage, then land was purchased, and today, part of the park has been completed.
On this day of July 1, the 94th anniversary of confederation, I think it is appropriate to express the hope, that in 1967, six years hence, or 30 years after development of this park was initiated, the 1937 dream will come true and Gatineau park will be completed.
Let us not forget that this is the only national park in the province of Quebec.
At this point, I should like to suggest to the minister and to the members of the national capital commission that they urge the federal government to approach the government of the province of Quebec and ask that the land now owned by the province be set aside for the Gatineau park.
This is certainly the best time to come to an agreement -with Quebec in that connection, for, today, Quebec is really part of the confederation.
Ten or 15 years ago, various members of the commission tried to reach an agreement with the province of Quebec with regard to provincially-owned land which could be used to complete the park development. But no agreement could be reached.

Supply-Public Works
I believe the commission should take further steps to settle this important question.
The agreement could be on two points. First of all, we should obtain for the park all the lands belonging to the lands and forest department of the province of Quebec; and secondly, the N.C.C. should let the province have the right of way which it holds on a property formerly owned by the Hull electric company, where the latter ran its street cars between Hull and Aylmer. Furthermore the town of Aylmer and all the area between Hull and Aylmer need a second highway.
I think the commission should take steps to make such an exchange with Quebec, thereby simultaneously solving two problems: that of the Gatineau park, and1 the traffic problem between Hull and Aylmer.
Mr. Chairman, in the last few years, the funds appropriated for the development of the Gatineau park have been reduced. I realize that some of the projects involved in the national capital development program are more urgent than others. However, in view of the present unemployment in the Hull district, the riding of Gatineau and the neighbouring area, it seems to me that the government should increase its expenses instead of reducing them. Such a development could provide a great deal of work for labourers. I feel that the commission authorities would be wise to undertake the continuation of the parkway that goes from Hull to the Champlain look-out because, after all, that is the first stretch of the Gatineau parkway. The commission should extend it not only to lake Philippe but to the north limit of the park in the riding of Pontiac.
However, I should like to express my appreciation to the national capital commission for having granted recently a contract for the paving of the road between Wakefield and Masham to lake Philippe. The house is no doubt aware of the fact that all necessary facilities are to be found at lake Philippe and that thousands of tourists spend their days and week ends at that lake. The paving of those three miles of road is truly beneficial to the people who go to that fine lake.
I would have a few suggestions to make to the commission concerning the development of that park. There are some 30 lakes within the park. Some of them are quite large and offer good fishing since tourists find there the species of fish they are looking for. We have in that park, only a few miles from the capital, salmon trout, bass, pike and pickerel.

In my opinion, the commission should have a biological survey carried out immediately in those lakes and have all non-sport fish destroyed. It should also see to the construction of a fish-breeding establishment in order to stock those lakes with appropriate fish. Thus we would have lakes well provided with fish for the tourists, when the construction of parkways and roads will have opened the area to the public.
I should like also to say a few words about the prison camp to be opened in a few days, if it is not already opened. It is located in the riding of Gatineau, or rather in the riding of Pontiac, but in the Gatineau park.
Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make on this subject. I am aware that the national capital commission is not responsible for this project for it comes under the Department of Justice. However, since it is essential that good relations exist between the national capital commission and those who reside near the park, I suggest the commission should not be responsible for this prisoners' camp.
People throughout the area are against the prison camp. The Gatineau county council, the chambers of commerce, schoolboards and town councils have passed resolutions which were sent to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) to protest the establishment of such a camp in the area.
Can you imagine, Mr. Chairman, what it means to have from 80 to 100 prisoners in such a camp? It means that work which should normally be done by local people, who have a right to work and a good many of whom are unemployed because they have agreed to work for the national capital commission for the building of this camp. Well, that work will not be carried out by them any more. In my region, we have unemployed heads of families to whom it is very difficult to explain that the government prefers to have the work done by prisoners, by former criminals rather than by our honest people. That is why I should not want the commission to bear the responsibility for that camp in Gatineau park. Fortunately, the camp will not be set up in the constituency of Gatineau, but rather in the Gatineau park, that is to say, in the constituency of Pontiac-Temisca-mingue. It is not for me to express here the views of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temis-camingue (Mr. Martineau), but I do know-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: He can express his own views.

-that some of the voters in the constituency of Pontiac-Temiscamingue, which is close to mine, came to see me to say they were not satisfied either. I should like the public to know that the commission is not responsible for the setting up of that camp.
Now, I would like to make a few more brief remarks in connection with zoning and building regulations in municipalities located within the national capital area. The N.C.C. makes available to municipalities the services of expert town planners for the preparation of zoning plans and proposals for building regulations.
It is deplorable that some municipalities within the limits of the national capital have no zoning nor building regulations. I understand that in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario some municipalities cannot afford the services of expert town-planners for that kind of work. But fortunately, within the limits of the national capital, services of such experts are offered free of charge to all municipal councils. I would ask the commission to exert pressure, or at least to do what can be done to inform the people in those various municipalities so that they will ask the commission for the services of the town planners to prepare adequate plans.
There are unfortunately, quite close to Hull city limits, villages which are developing into real slum villages. Why? Because those municipalities have no zoning or building regulations to control building in the limits of their own territory. I
I know that at this time there is serious work being done in Quebec to help and advise municipalities in taking zoning and urban development measures. I hope the commission will do its best to see that all the municipalities in the national capital area have their own zoning and construction programs as soon as possible and that the bylaws they adopt are strictly enforced.
No match-box post offices.

Mr. Chairman, I had no intention of speaking on this item, but in view of the remarks just made by my hon. colleague from Gatineau (Mr. Leduc), I feel I should give the house my views on this matter.
It goes without saying that I fully agree with some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Gatineau, and especially with those pertaining to the beauties of the Gatineau park and of the Pontiac-Temiscamingue and Gatineau ridings. As a matter of fact, I am the first to support his views. I fully support some of his suggestions concerning the development of the park and the building of roads through it, so that the greatest possible number of citizens may enjoy the natural beauties that are to be found there. I am happy to say to the hon. gentleman that his comments on this matter are greatly appreciated.
However, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member raised a question about which I feel, he did not do justice in his speech. I refer to the use of prisoners to carry out work within the Gatineau park.
I should ask the hon. member for Gatineau to refer particularly to the statements made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) about this matter. In reply to a question about the consequences of setting up correctional working camps, and more particularly about the work to be carried out in the Gatineau park, in co-operation with the national capital commission, the Minister of Justice stated as follows, as recorded on page 1 of the English Hansard for December 21, 1960:
The government believes in the principles underlying such rehabilitation projects and their use for resources conservation purposes. However, in the study of each particular project, we require that the following test be applied: Is it expected that the project, within about ten years, would be carried out by regular workers and paid for out of public funds? If so, it is not undertaken by prisoners.
When discussing the estimates of the justice department the same question was dealt with and the Minister of Justice stated on June 9, 1961, as will be found in Hansard:
During the coming months it is intended to place the emphasis upon the development of minimum security institutions. The committee will have

Supply-Public Works
gathered from my previous remarks that the pressure for medium security institutions has in some measure been relieved, and our greatest need is for institutions in which the benefits of minimum security conditions can be brought to bear upon those inmates who have responded to our new rehabilitation methods. The necessary provision has now been made so that, across the country, we shall be opening five correctional work camps, each designed to provide accommodation and training for 80 inmates. These camps-
The minister there listed the various locations where those camps would be set up and mentioned the Gatineau park, in Quebec.
And the minister went on:
I would like to assure the house that none of the men held in these institutions will he engaged upon work which would deprive other Canadians of employment. None of the projects which they undertake would be commenced within ten years if they had to be paid for out of tax moneys at the current rates of civilian pay.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Justice indicated on two different occasions that the work carried out under that program would be of a kind which, anyway, is not planned for the next ten years and far from delaying the development of the Gatineau park, will rather accelerate this project.
Mr. Chairman, I understand that no unemployed worker in the area will be deprived of a job, because of those works the purpose of which is to establish those very facilities the hon. member for Gatineau himself has been asking for.
In addition, there is no doubt that the establishment of a prison camp will create jobs for a number of guards and caterers, the latter having to supply the inmates of the institution with the required services and commodities. I therefore feel that if we adopt that position, far from depriving the local people of jobs, we will on the contrary create additional jobs.
Mr. Chairman, I am glad to see that recently some officers of the Department of Justice went to my hon. friend's riding to explain the objectives of that department when they establish such correctional work camps.
The hon. member for Gatineau has referred to complaints he has apparently received from his constituents. Personally, I can say here that I have never received any complaint from anyone in my constituency. Quite to the contrary, municipal authorities wrote to congratulate this government for undertaking work that will considerably help the develop-

ment of an area which, in the opinion of all, including the hon. member for Gatineau, is quite promising from the viewpoint of tourist attractions of all kinds.
I also take this opportunity to ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) to see that the national capital commission carries on with this worth-while project of the Gatineau park development, so that not only the citizens of our district, but all the citizens of this country may fully benefit from the natural attractions of the Gatineau park, which all of us praise.

I rise just to ask a question or two of the minister. However, before doing so I must express my full appreciation of the work that has been undertaken throughout the years by the capital commission for the planned beautification of Ottawa and its environs. As a matter of fact I have no hesitation in saying that practically everything Ottawa has with respect to beautiful gardens, drives, lawns and parks is the result of the activity of the capital commission. I think much credit should be given to that robust, energetic and very capable person General Kennedy and his colleagues.
By the way, Mr. Chairman, I must be getting on in years because 44 years ago I never thought I would speak a good word for a general again after being carted about 100 miles across France in a G.S. wagon in order to be court-martialled for supposedly giving a platoon a wrong order in action. As soon as the court saw me, of course, they knew I was innocent and the charge was dismissed.
However, I must say also that I wish to compliment the person, whoever it is, who is responsible for the decoration around the grounds of parliament for this holiday season. I hear some comment and I can well understand it; but honestly I am giving my opinion. I think we have more colour, greater effect, and more holiday and festive atmosphere for the least expense than we have had for a good many years. I have had a look at these decorations. 1 find that, best of all, the flags, the poles and the portable cement blocks will serve for many future national holidays, festive occasions, welcomes to visitors from overseas and so on. I like the idea of being able to use these materials over and over

again. As I say, I have seen some heavy expenditures, on occasions, on things which could not be used again.
Now I come to my question. I have had a number of visits from residents in the Sussex street district, in addition to considerable correspondence from them. I have heard from the owners of property and private homes on Sussex Street who are concerned about the possibility of the expropriation of that property by the national capital commission. This is a natural concern. I understand these people are reconciled to their property being expropriated if they can be convinced that it is necessary for the beautification of Ottawa as part of the national capital commission plan, but they have heard reports from reliable sources that over the years representatives of the French government have been approaching the appropriate persons in the federal government with a view to having a site expropriated opposite the present French embassy for the building of a chancellery. These people are concerned if property is to be expropriated for that purpose. I understand and there are a number of civil servants who have reason to believe that representations have been made at a high level for the expropriation of property for that purpose.
These people claim there is ample room in the grounds of the French embassy for extra buildings to serve the great and friendly nation of France. I can hardly credit why people should come to me on occasions in respect to such matters as this, but, as I say, I have had correspondence dealing with this question, in addition to a number of visits, and I undertook to raise the matter in the house and ask the minister whether it is correct to say that representations have been made on behalf of the French government in this connection to any department of the government of Canada for the expropriation of certain land for the construction of a chancellery or other building for the French government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Kootenay West for his remarks. The national capital commission over-all plan has for many years envisaged making Sussex drive from the parliament buildings to government house a processional drive or, as I stated at one time, we should like to preserve the good that was there and improve what is not good. This is a plan which has long been outstanding. I can tell the hon. member that as far as any government outside Canada is concerned representations such as he has described
Supply-Public Works
have played no part in any such plan. No representations were made by the commission at the time this plan was envisaged. If any formal representations have been made on behalf of any foreign government they have not been made to the national capital commission.
Perhaps I might say one further thing. I am not, in all humility, as the minister responsible for the national capital commission, able to accept credit for the wonderful decorations outside the parliament buildings to help us celebrate Dominion day. However, in all modesty, I can accept congratulations as the Minister of Public Works.

I have no desire to debate matters having to do with the Department of Public Works, but I cannot help observing that there have been small criticisms of certain actions such as the tearing up of the lovely lawns cared for by the national capital commission. The Department of Public Works has come along to dig ditches, excavate and put in temporary wires. There are all kinds of side issues and altogether the situation is not as happy as the minister would have us think. Perhaps if I press the subject further, Mr. Chairman, you would call me out of order, and I am sure that in the spirit of the holiday no one would like that to happen.
I should like to ask the minister a few questions with regard to the position of chairman of the commission. It is very important, I think the committee would agree, that the chairman of the board should be endowed with a blend of natural qualities. He should be sufficiently artistic to visualize development of an area and at the same time he must be practical enough to be able to carry out the practical work required to be done. Then, above all other capacities, he must be able to co-ordinate his activities with those of the other authorities, provincial and municipal, engaged in his field in such a way as to obtain the greatest effect from the total resources available. It seems to me that all this requires great qualities of mind and character including patience and, indeed, wisdom beyond that given to most of us.
We have had a succession of very fine chairmen of this commission and I hope the one to be appointed in the future will be of the same high calibre. The present chairman has been the general manager of the commission for many years and I think we would all wish to publicly acknowledge the good work he has done over the whole of this period. My understanding is that his present position as chairman is of a temporary nature and that his tenure expires some time this autumn. I assume the minister is not able to tell us at this stage the name of whoever is destined to be his

Supply-Public Works
successor, but ii the hon. gentleman has any information on this subject which he feels he can properly release at this time I should be glad to have it.
While I am making reference to the present chairman of the commission in his former capacity as general manager, I might also refer to the fact that we have with us today on the floor of the chamber, I believe, for the first time, the new general manager. I can only say that I wish him well in the years ahead. I wish him all those qualities which are required to carry on this work, not the least of which may be patience.
I do not know whether the minister wishes to answer my questions as they arise. I have one or two more to ask.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I shall answer them all at the
same time.

I should appreciate it if the minister could throw some light on this question of the chairmanship of the commission, because I can tell the hon. gentleman that if the appointment is not made before the election there will be appointed a man of the very finest calibre; and I hope that even if the appointment is made before the election the position will be filled by a man of the same qualities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman this question. If, after the election, he were to find himself unemployed would he be a candidate for the position?

No. But after the election, my leader authorizes me to say, I shall have the fullest possible say about the appointment of the chairman and he will be of the highest calibre.
I wish to raise another matter having to do with the composition of the board. The composition of the board has been changed from time to time but the latest change made involved the dropping of the representatives of the cities of Ottawa and Hull. While these are only two of many municipalities involved they are the two largest. I like to stress every time I speak on this subject the necessity for good co-ordination and good relationships among the municipal bodies concerned and this commission. I would hope that the minister would consider this point and, overlooking whatever the vicissitudes may be at any given moment in dealing with this subject, would consider submitting to the house an amendment to the act providing that the officers holding the positions of mayor of Hull and mayor of Ottawa be on the commission. That is something of which we should not lose sight and I hope the minister will give it consideration.

There is one other question which I should like to raise. The whole question of expropriation has become increasingly important these last few years as the use of expropriation has increased sharply for national capital commission purposes, for federal public works' purposes, and indeed in the provincial government legislative field, as well as for municipal purposes. This is a difficult subject and there is no doubt at all that experience has revealed many weaknesses in the existing procedure. I had understood that new legislation on this subject was being brought forward at this session. While it has not been brought forward I wonder whether the minister would state exactly what the position of the government is with respect to it. It seems to me that this legislation is overdue and that a statement by the minister should be made at this session. These days when we hear so much about the bill of rights, I sometimes think, in keeping with the spirit of the bill of rights, we might modernize this legislation a bit to bring it more up to date.
Would the minister advise the house what acreage in the green belt development has been acquired and what acreage is yet to be acquired, and, of the acreage yet to be acquired, what portion of it is now under expropriation proceedings, in what area and to what extent is it intended to continue to attempt to negotiate without expropriation? I would ask him to give us the amount paid to date for property acquired for the green belt as well as his estimate of the amount required to complete the acquisition of the balance of the property.
Then, as to Sussex street, I have some specific questions I should like to ask. What is the estimated cost of expropriation of land by the national capital commission between Sussex drive and Thomas street? Is the minister in a position to develop further at this stage the plans for the use of the lands to be expropriated?
Will any of the buildings on the lands to be expropriated be preserved, or is it intended to replace them all? Will the minister clarify the position of the government concerning the future use of this land for embassy sites? There has been talk from time to time, one way and another, on this point and the situation is quite obscure. Perhaps he could clarify it.
Then there is the question that arises as to whether or not any of this area is to be used as a park site. If that is so, would the minister elaborate a bit on the nature of the park development to take place there, and tell us what expected use will be made of that park, bearing in mind its proximity to other park areas, namely, Rockcliffe park.

Has the minister considered the possibility under our housing legislation of proceeding to develop part of the area outside the area being taken by the national capital commission so that the housing standards in that part of the area could be raised? The standards in part of the area now are very good but there are some other areas in close proximity where the standards are not as good as they might be. It seems to me the housing legislation we have would permit of an advantageous use of funds voted under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in conjunction with the provinces and municipalities to undertake certain works to bring that adjacent area into better relationship to the proposed new development for Sussex street.
Perhaps at this stage I should give the minister an opportunity to reply to my questions. I have attempted to state them concisely and specifically but I realize they have covered a somewhat wide range.

That is something new. The acreage to be acquired is 673 parcels of 6,818 acres. We have under option at the present time 72 parcels of 2,860 acres. The amount already purchased involves 598 parcels of 24,722 acres.
The Sussex drive development program, as the hon. member for Ottawa West knows, is still under consideration. When the original Greber plan of the national capital commission, or the federal district commission as it was then called, was brought in some years ago it contemplated embassy sites somewhere along Sussex street. But I can assure the hon. member that during my tenure of office in any event, the national capital commission has made no such plans nor has it come forward with any such plans.
I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa West that we should have a very distinguished man to succeed General Howard Kennedy, of whom I think very highly, and also Mr. A. K. Hay, who has given a lifetime of distinguished service to the national capital commission. Mr. Alan Hay is a wonderful type of man. It is a great credit to any country to have such a public servant. It is through his own insistent request that we shall be forced to allow him to terminate his services as chairman of this commission on September 30 of this year. It was only at our urgent request that he has stayed on as long as he has. I hope by that time to be able to announce to parliament and to the people of Canada the appointment of a distinguished successor who will maintain the excellent tradition established by the former chairmen of this commission.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Ottawa West advocating-I take it he was advocating it-the appointment of my distinguished friend and his political enemy, the mayor of Ottawa, to the national capital

Supply-Public Works
commission. If that was what he was doing today it is unique. It shows how broadminded he really is. I can say though that it was our predecessors in office, the St. Laurent government and Mr. St. Laurent himself who insisted that the National Capital Act should be amended so that neither the mayor of Ottawa nor the mayor of Hull would of necessity or as a matter of right be members of this commission. The former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, felt that there would be a distinct conflict of interest between the duties of the mayor of Ottawa as such, or the mayor of Hull as such, and the interests of the national capital commission as such. Therefore, section 3 of the act states that as a statutory right Ottawa should have at least two representatives on the commission and Hull one. I think this answers the questions the hon. member asked.

There is one point I think I should clarify. I refer to the minister's reference to the former prime minister. I think his comment went farther than the facts warrant. I am aware that the draft bill prepared by the previous government did not make provision for the appointment of the mayor of Ottawa and the mayor of Hull as members of the commission. I am aware of that fact but I believe that a more careful examination will indicate to the minister that his other remarks when he was purporting to speak for the former prime minister were not in accordance with the facts. I think he would not wish to leave them just the way they were expressed. I think on examination he will find the facts are more closely as 1 state them on that point. I am aware that the bill submitted, but not dealt with by the former government, did omit the provision for the appointment for the mayor of Ottawa and the mayor of Hull to the commission, but I am not by any means satisfied that the bill would not have been changed, or that the provision would not have been changed, before or during its submission to the House of Commons. I think the minister will agree with me that it is fair to leave the matter that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May I say one word there. I think I know whereof I speak. We inherited the draft from the St. Laurent government and all we did was to put it through. This was the suggestion of the former prime minister himself. It was his suggestion that the change I have outlined should take place.

I thought I made it clear that this clause was in the draft bill prepared by the former government, but to go beyond that and say what the minister has said were the views of the prime minister of Canada at that time is to say something that I

think is not in accordance with the facts. It certainly is not in accordance with my understanding and discussion at that time. The minister went beyond what I thought was the position of the prime minister of Canada at that time, who was pretty careful in these things. I do not want to rethresh old straw because I do not think it is germane at the moment. Surely the minister would wish to leave the matter there. My remarks still stand about him giving this matter further consideration in the future. Despite the views the minister may have at the moment I think this must be viewed as a long term matter. We have constantly to keep before us the absolute necessity of effective co-ordination and good working relationships with the councils of all municipalities in the area.
There is one other matter that the minister passed over a bit lightly, namely the Expropriation Act. While technically the Expropriation Act may come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice, it is almost of exclusive concern of the Minister of Public Works because he heads up the two large expropriating bodies in Canada, namely the national capital commission and the Department of Public Works. I would hope that he would concern himself directly with this problem because the legislation does need modernizing. While it may be a difficult subject to deal with I would hope that he would address himself to the problem. I ask him to do so. I remind him that he seems to have overlooked a very important fact in this connection, namely that very early in this session my colleague from Essex East introduced a bill to amend the Expropriation Act in one very important particular. I think I should draw this to the attention of the minister because he seems to have overlooked it. The explanatory note of the bill reads as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to amend the Expropriation Act so as to require the minister, in the name of the crown, to give notice of intention to all interested parties of the crown's intention to take or acquire lands or any interest therein.
This procedure would be in accordance with the principles recognized and declared in the Canadian Bill of Rights.
On this anniversary of the bill of rights I think the Minister of Public Works would do well to take note of the point raised by my colleague in Bill No. C-63. I hope that he will have it embodied in the new bill when it comes forward.

Before the item carries may I say I have been interested in the remarks of the hon. members from the capital area. I am

sorry there are not more of them with us today because a number of things have been raised today that would be of interest to them and of which the commission should take note.
I congratulate the commission on the work that it has done, particularly in this adventure for citizenship in which the Rotary club and the national capital commission have jointly co-operated because it has given opportunity to members from areas other than those directly connected with the national capital commission jurisdiction to see some of the work and projects that are being undertaken. I also congratulate them on the tour of the national capital commission area which they arranged recently, advantage of which was taken by some members of the house. It provided an opportunity to see some of the developments that are taking place in the area.
I recommend strongly that the request of the hon. member for Ottawa West that Charlotte Whitton be appointed to the commission be given consideration by the government. This might be a hardship on the commission because city council and the board of control have undergone hardship, but I do think there is an obligation to bring together the commission and the city of Ottawa. The beautification of the city of Ottawa and works in that regard are in the main the responsibility of the national capital commission and I think there should be more cooperation with respect to some of the things that are going on in the area.
I support the hon. member for Ottawa West with regard to the matter of expropriation and also the question of how extensive the green belt is going to be. I have received some representations regarding disputes from lawyers in the area involved in certain property deals. Real estate deals are going on continually in what is considered to be the green belt area and these lawyers find that commercial enterprises are being established in an area where it had been indicated that expropriation was going to take place. The hon. member for Carleton does not need to shake his head. The area I am referring to is in the county of Russell across the Rideau river. There is considerable misunderstanding on the part of people there. They are not being allowed to build homes on the land while at the same time motels, golf driving ranges and so on are being established. In my opinion and in the opinion of many of the lawyers involved this has created an opportunity for some people to make money to which they probably should not have been entitled.
I should also like to congratulate the commission on the parks that come under their jurisdiction. I would simply request that they 90205-6-466

take care that they do not follow the practice of the province of Ontario which has continually increased the entrance fee to its parks over the past few years. If the government is going to provide the commission with close to $9 million this year, the parks should be made available to the largest number of people possible so that they can enjoy the benefits. I do not believe it is expected that these parks will be self sustaining. We intend to continue to spend money for the maintenance and upkeep of these parks because it is not expected that the revenue will be sufficient for that purpose.
There has been a great deal of discussion this afternoon about Sussex street. I think Sussex street is not in too bad shape. What I object to particularly is the condition of Wellington street in front of the parliament buildings. It seems to me that some consideration should be given to this street by the national capital commission because they seem to be one of the very few departments of government that really spend a lot of money, time and effort on planning. If they decide to do something about Wellington street, possibly it is within their jurisdiction to consider the matter of providing parking facilities off parliament hill. There seems to be no reason why they could not erect a building to provide parking facilities for the cars that normally park on the hill. Fees could be collected for the cars stored in such a building. Certainly the people who work here, senators and even members of parliament should be able to pay for parking facilities.
It seems to me that expediency has prevailed over aesthetic values because the hill should be a place of trees, gardens and parks. Many of the little parking lots that have been established on the hill have been placed there as temporary expedients pending the solution of what is obviously a very complicated problem. If the commission were to make a strong enough recommendation for off-the-hill parking, I think arrangements could probably be made for facilities on the other side of Wellington street that would meet my desire to have attractive government buildings on that street and at the same time would be functional as far as parking is concerned. The problem is a temporary one but so far it has not been solved. The amount of parking on the hill is very restricted and cannot be extended to any great extent. In my view the present situation detracts from the appearance of parliament hill.
There is another problem to which I should like the commission to give some consideration. Complaints have been made to me by a number of people respecting certain areas

Supply-Public Works
in Gatineau park. In particular I have reference to the Ottawa ski club area. I have received many complaints from young people that if they want to go into that area in the winter they have to pay a sum of money to enter the area, even though the commission assists in maintaining the roads. I think this problem could easily be eliminated if the commission would sit down with officials of the Ottawa ski club and other organizations similarly involved. I believe that much more co-operative arrangements could be worked out which would serve the needs of the community. It may be that the commission might see fit to buy the Ottawa ski club facilities because it seems to me that they are winter facilities used by the people for their enjoyment in the same way that the facilities of a place like lac Philippe are used by the people in the summer. Mr. Chairman, I should like the minister to explain very briefly what control the national capital commission has over the location and design of new government buildings. I am particularly interested in the national war museum and I have brought up this matter on several occasions. I know that the operation of the museum comes under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and that the matter of a new building would come under the Department of Public Works. However, if the national capital commission has any say as to the location and planning of new buildings, can the minister tell us whether they have any plan in mind for the provision of a new building for the national war museum? Mr. Chairman, the province of Quebec has 25 per cent of Canada's productive forests. Forests are most important to this country. First, they are a source of substantial income for the pulp, paper and lumber industry. Second, there is a close relation between our forests and our waterways, because the former control and regulate the flow of surface waters and at the same time constitute water reserves. Third, they are ideal hunting and fishing grounds. So we must protect our forests.
In addition to the funds spent by the provincial and federal governments through the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming), we have 4-H clubs accomplishing fine work in co-operation with the Quebec government in particular.
Our legislation should me made more stringent in order to put a stop to the negligence of those who are responsible for forest fires.
Second, the sale of Christmas trees should be closely supervised. In my opinion, there is abuse in that field.
Third, our youth should be taught in schools to respect our trees.
I should like to ask the minister whether he has taken steps through his officials or the civil service commission, to recruit forestry engineers or scientists in the universities of the province of Quebec, in view of the fact that there are not enough bilingual civil servants in the forestry department considering the important role which the province of Quebec is called upon to play since it has 25 per cent of Canada's productive forests.
I should also like to ask the minister whether the government intends to appoint, in the near future, a French speaking and bilingual assistant deputy minister to the Department of Forestry.
(Text):

I cannot let the estimates of this important department go by without making a few observations. I rise also to extend to the new minister, or shall I say the first minister, of forestry, my sincere congratulations upon his appointment and best wishes for the successful administration

of a department which is of great importance to my constituency. My constituency is economically dependent, to a very large extent, on forests and forest products.
I had the great pleasure, Mr. Chairman, of introducing the minister to the people of Fort William on his first visit to the lake-head on May 24 when he addressed the Fort William Canadian club. It was a gathering of a cross-section of the business, professional and trades people of both cities, including a special group interested in the forest industry. Measured by the reaction of press, radio and television, the minister's visit was a great success. His speech, which contained promises of plans for rapid expansion of research activities in forest products marketing, was well received. I should say also that his visit provided an excellent opportunity for the minister to get personally acquainted with some of our people directly and indirectly interested in the success of federal forestry policy.
The pulp and paper industry is one of the major employers of labour in our district. The same can be said, of course, for the whole of northwestern Ontario. A great number of our farmers are dependent for a goodly portion of their income upon the operation of woodlots. I express the hope, Mr. Chairman, that the minister, who has many years of practical experience in woods operations, will take into account the welfare of these farmers by rendering some form of federal assistance in marketing their wood. I express the hope, too, that he will explore the possibility for improving production and management as well as the possibility of developing an industry related to farming in forestry. These possibilities should be carefully investigated with a view to bettering rural community life by stabilizing farm population. An aggressive federal Department of Forestry, in co-operation with the provinces, may well undertake these developments with a view to bringing about a new era for the woodlot farmers of Canada.
The government should make credit available to these woodlot farmers to improve their holdings. A better system of approving loans than that which the farm credit corporation used in assessing the value of farm holdings in the district of Thunder bay should be adopted. Because of the distorted method of determining whether or not an applicant is eligible for a loan, very few applicants were able to qualify.
An economic survey of northwestern Ontario issued by the Ontario department of economics contains some very interesting data concerning the income of pulp and paper workers, which is shown to be well 90205-6-466J
Supply-Forestry
above the average for industrial and construction workers. The forests of Thunder bay have built the towns of Red Rock, Terrace Bay, Nipigon, Long Lac and Marathon. There should be no need, really, to stress the importance of the pulp and paper and lumber industries to the well being of Canada. The evidence of this fact is there for everyone to see. The forest industry alone of the great national, basic industries receives no subsidy. It is not seeking any. Yet, when you compare the annual production from the forest industry with the annual production of agriculture and mining, you find without doubt this industry produces the greatest total buying power and contributes vastly more to a favourable trade balance, supports the greatest export trade and produces the largest tax revenues if we combine the taxes levied by both provincial and federal governments.
Our federal government spends approximately $6 million each year on forest administration and research, $25 million on mining administration, research and subsidies; $80 million in agriculture administration, research and subsidies.
What are the revenues from these basic industries? Federal and provincial governments together receive a $230 million annual revenue from agriculture of which they spend $150 million. From the forests these two senior governments receive $275 million of which they spend a combined total of $45 million. From the figures it can be seen that we can afford to be a little more generous towards the basic industry for which we should be very thankful.
Mr. D. W. Ambridge, president of Abitibi Pulp and Paper Company, speaking at the annual lakehead district credit union banquet, recently recounted some of his observations on a recent European tour that he had made as a member of a government delegation to investigate common market countries. Mr. Ambridge made the statement that amazing development was evident in Europe. I wish to quote from the Thursday, June 22 issue of the Fort William Times Journal just a few remarks from his address:
"-Today Europe's economy is progressing much faster than ours," he remarked.
He said he was impressed with the close co-operation between government, industry and labour.
"What we've got to realize in Canada ... is that we have no great ticket to prosperity."
Mr. Ambridge said Finland will soon launch 600,000 tons of newsprint on the world market and has every intention of pushing out Canada. He added the Finns built paper mills with loans from the world bank as a step in alleviating the unemployment situation.
"We have to take note of these things," he urged. "We have to be alive to the fact we can not prosper without effort."
