Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Will he say who that was he was quoting? I refer to what he has just finished reading.

Mr. Chairman, may I also join with my colleagues in extending congratulations to the minister on his appointment to this very important portfolio of Minister of Forestry. Since his appointment, the minister has visited our province of British Columbia and his speeches have been well received. I wish to assure him that we look forward to seeing more of him.
I wish to say a few words on the need to provide greater and better forest fire protection. In view of the great number of forest fires which are raging across the country at
Supply-Forestry
this moment, I suggest that what I have to say can be classed as urgent. British Columbia has a very large stake in timber and in forestry products. The value of our lumber production and saw mill products in 1958 amounted to $356 million according to figures prepared by the dominion bureau of statistics. In 1960 we expect that the value of our lumber production will have reached an astronomical $738 million, an increase of $68 million over 1959. The next most productive province in 1958, by way of comparison, was Quebec with $76 million. It is therefore obvious that forestry is British Columbia's major industry. However, this major industry suffers very greatly each year because of inadequate forest fire protection. On a national basis, the cost of forest fire fighting amounted to $7.7 million in 1958, and the total damage and fire fighting costs for the same year were calculated to be $22.2 million, an amount almost twice the total budget for the Department of Forestry for this year.
We in British Columbia suffered disastrously in 1958 because in that year we had the worst fire season in history. Fire fighting costs and damage amounted to $13 million, almost equal to the total budget for this department. Huge though these sums might be, they still do not take into account such value as damage to soil, streamflow, wildlife, recreation and tourist facilities. Recent events from British Columbia to Newfoundland indicate that this is going to be another very bad year for this country, because the June 24 issue of the Vancouver Province devoted almost its entire front page to news about forest fires. The headline was, and I quote: "Huge Water Bomber Crashes, 4 Die". Another headline was "Flying 'Fire Engine' Just a Ghost Now." And then, on the second page were more headlines, and I quote again: "Forest Risk puts 3,000 Out of Work." On the same page was another headline reading: "Newfoundland Fires Drive 2,000 from Homes." If I remember correctly, yesterday's banner from the Toronto Telegram read: "Forest Fires Worst in Years."
What, then, can we do to provide adequate fire protection bearing in mind that the major share of the responsibility lies with the provincial government? I think, Mr. Chairman, that the minister should consider the establishment of a national forest fire service similar in concept to our recently established Canadian marine service. This will be composed of a highly mobile fleet of suitable aircraft such as Otters and helicop-

Supply-Forestry
ters. The usefulness of such an airborne fire fighting service has been well demonstrated in the province of Ontario, where up to this present year there has been a steady decrease in the number of forest fires, climaxed in 1959 when only 5,279 acres were burnt over. This figure represents the lowest loss in three decades and it clearly demonstrates what can be done by a program of public education and effective fire fighting measures. Ontario has a fleet of six Otters and 39 Beavers which are specially designed to scoop up water as the aircraft taxis over the lake. The water is then dispersed over the fire in an effective wetting action. In many cases two or three well placed loads have doused the fire to such an extent that an incoming ground crew had only to extinguish the smouldering embers. So effective has been this technique that the fire loss in Ontario has been reduced from an average of 75 acres per fire in the 1949-58 decade to an average of five acres per fire in 1959.
We in British Columbia have had similar good results with water bombing. The water bomber which crashed on June 24 started its work in very dramatic fashion. On June 17, one week before it crashed, the Vancouver Province carried the following article:
Water bomber proves worth by hitting fire
The big Martin Mars water bomber passed its first real test Friday when nearly 50,000 gallons were dropped on a difficult forest fire at Espinosa inlet, near Tahsis, on Vancouver island.
It made eight drops to dampen and cool the fire sufficiently to allow ground crews in to control it.
The fire, on three acres of a steep, narrow valley in an operation of the Stoltze and Sons Logging Company Limited, was fanned by strong winds and quickly covered about 40 acres.
This technique of containment emphasizes that there must be two ingredients for effective fire protection, namely, early spotting of the fire, and immediate preventive action by air, followed by prompt action by ground personnel. Because ground personnel must be brought in to ensure that the fire is completely out, I suggest that helicopters should be an integral part of the national forest fire service.
I think that the establishment of such a service is well within the resources of the federal government. I note that approximately $6.8 million will be contributed this year to the provinces for fire protection, forest inventory, reforestry action and other aspects of forest management. Twenty four Otters with spare parts would cost only $3.6 million. We could have these aircraft stationed across Canada at strategic locations.
More might be necessary, but 24 would be a very good start. We could enter an agreement with the provinces concerned to fly and maintain the aircraft, or we could assume full responsibility for this service and reduce the yearly grants which we would make in the future to the provinces.
I can envisage all sorts of interesting arrangements being worked out with the provinces. For example, the provinces could provide the helicopters and the manpower required to deal with the fires on the ground because obtaining crews could be accomplished more easily by the local authorities. If we had an effective air fire service then fires would be checked in their early stages. We would not require the large number of men required in the past, some of whom were not trained in this activity and were often commandeered to do this type of thing. A small highly trained corps of fire fighters working in conjunction with the air service which I have suggested should go a long way toward reducing the damage caused by forest fires.
The minister announced in Nanaimo in April of this year that army and air force personnel would be available to help fight forest fires. I am pleased with that announcement, particularly as I urged this move last year during the debate on the estimates of the Department of National Defence. However, I have had second thoughts on this proposal because, if we were to use service personnel and aircraft not specifically designed for fire fighting we might be depriving the armed forces of men and equipment at a time when they should be deployed elsewhere. However, until such time as we do establish an alternative we, of course, welcome the assistance of the army and the air force. None the less, I think that a separate service is preferable, and my suggestion of creating a national forest fire service has the advantage of providing not only a further stimulus to our aircraft industry but also something which is of particular and urgent national need.

Mr. Chairman, we are at present on item No. 1 of the estimates of the new Department of Forestry. Some would have preferred it to be named the "Department of Forest Research" or "Department of Silviculture" since paragraph 5 of section 92 of the British North America Act gives the

provinces the exclusive power to administer as they see fit the forests within their boundaries and the federal government has responsibility in that field only as concerns the administration of forests in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Pursuant to Bill C-82, clause 6, 1960, an act respecting the Department of Forestry, the federal government:
Shall provide for the conduct of research relating to the protection, management and utilization of the forest resources;
May undertake, promote or recommend measures for the encouragement of public co-operation in the protection and wise use of the forest resources. With the approval of the governor in council, may enter into agreements with the government of any province, etc.-
Mr. Chairman, forest industry occupies a most important position in the economy of my riding, of the province of Quebec and Canada as a whole.
It gives me pleasure to congratulate the first incumbent of the portfolio of the new Department of Forestry, the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Flemming) and I know that he has had practical experience in the production and marketing of forest products.
Mr. Chairman, over 40 per cent of the total area of the ten provinces is productive forest lands. It is nearly four times the area under cultivation, which gives an idea of the extent of our forest resources.
The pulp and paper industry is Canada's foremost manufacturing industry, and the lumbering, plywood and veneer industries are also very important.
Those industries are spread out across Canada from coast to coast, and apart from producing materials of great value, they rank among our main sources of employment.
Mr. Chairman, wood, wood products and paper are responsible for a much greater part of Canada's active trade balance than any other group of goods registered in federal statistics. Moreover, a considerable part of this active trade balance is made up of American funds.
In September 1959, the world food and agricultural organization produced a report on paper and paper products and stated, in brief, that the demand for paper and paper products, which was of the order of 56 million metric tons in 1955, would reach 88 million metric tons by 1965 and 134 million metric tons by 1975.
Supply-Forestry
Mr. Chairman, Canada now supplies approximately 16 per cent of the world demand. If we want to maintain that share, we shall have to sell 14 million metric tons by 1965, which means raising our production by 50 per cent in relation to the basic year 1955. Around 1975, we will have to supply 21 million metric tons, which means raising our production by 123 per cent in relation to the basic year.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to the introduction, on page 1, of "The Outlook for the Canadian Forest Industries", published in March 1957 by the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, and I quote:
Even in Canada, few realize the country's dependence upon its forest resources. Great construction projects, especially in connection with power, metal mining, oil and, recently, natural gas, have received great publicity. Yet they are small by comparison. Today, one of every 12 Canadians working in the nation's goods-producing industries is concerned with forestry or the manufacture of forest products. More than one third of Canada's total export earnings comes from the sale elsewhere of logs, paper, wood pulp, and lumber and its related products. Of all the manufacturing industries in Canada, that of pulp and paper stands first in terms of wages paid, first in new investment and first in net value of output. Its production in dollar terms is greater than that of the nation's wheat crop; more than twice that of all the nation's metal mines. In 1954, Canada's saw mills, with the second largest industrial wage bill, ran third in export earnings and fourth in net value of production.
Mr. Chairman, at this point of our discussion on the estimates of the Department of Forestry, I should like to give some figures concerning the forest industry, first of all with regard to the number of establishments, and then with regard to the number of people employed in those industries and the salaries and wages paid. Those figures, which relate to the year 1959, were given to me by the dominion bureau of statistics, forest products division.
Mr. Chairman, the first figures I quote are in relation to the whole of Canada and the second to the province of Quebec which I represent here like other hon. members.
In 1959, the lumber industry in Canada comprised 8,885 different firms, 1,575 of which were in the province of Quebec.
As far as the pulp and paper industry is concerned, we had 127 mills in Canada, of which 54 were located in Quebec.
Canadian industries using wood as their raw material numbered 4,079 of which 1,504 were in Quebec.

Veneer and plywotfd plants numbered 72 in Canada and 24 in the province of Quebec.
The following figures, Mr. Chairman, concern the number of persons employed as well as the salaries and wages paid by those industries.
As far as the forest industry proper is concerned, the number of employees in 1959, equalled 82,551 men in a single year, for a total amount of salaries and wages of $347,406,000. For the same industry, we had in the province of Quebec, for the equivalent of a year, 30,850 employees who earned a total of $117,741,000.
In 1959, there were 65,028 people working in the pulp and paper industry and the total salaries paid out was $322,311,000. As for the province of Quebec, there were 27,239 employees who earned a total of $131,913,000.
In 1959, 48,659 people derived their livelihood from the lumber industry in Canada and the total salaries paid out by that industry amounted to $144,759,000. For the same period, that industry employed 7,963 people in the province of Quebec and paid a total of $16,900,070 in salaries.
There were in the country 11,607 people with gross earnings of $40,600,058 in the veneer and plywood industry. In the province of Quebec, that industry ensured the livelihood of 2,609 people and paid out a total of $7.3 million in salaries.
In 1958, there were 73,159 people employed in the industry where wood is used as a raw material; they earned $226,882,000. The corresponding figures for the province of Quebec were 23,464 employees and $64,636,000.
Mr. Chairman, the forest industry is most important in the riding of Labelle which I represent in this house. On March 23 last, I stated in the house, as reported on page 3284 of Hansard, during consideration of another department's estimates, that many farmers of my riding have to work in the forest industry to supplement the insufficiency of the income they get from the sale of their agricultural products. That industry employs several thousand people. There is a veneer and plywood mill in Mont Laurier, a furniture manufacture in L'Annonciation and, in Thurso, where I live, a pulp and paper mill and a cabinet-making department. Besides, there are several saw mills, planing mills and sash and door manufacturers elsewhere.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about the sale and distribution of forestry products. I regret that the federal government has not seen fit to take action on a recommendation we find on page 669 of the third report of the mines, forests and waters committee which was tabled in the house on July 4, 1959 and which reads as follows:
Your committee feels that Canada cannot afford to neglect the vast potential Asiatic markets for the sale of lumber and pulpwood. It recommends that open-minded negotiations be undertaken with those countries. Our traditional share of the British and American markets is undergoing a change and we should look into the situation. Your committee recommends the establishment of a sales branch within the proposed forestry department. Such a branch would second the efforts of the Department of Trade and Commerce to promote the sale of our wood products.
Mr. Chairman, the sale of lumber and of our veneer and plywood products faces stronger competition on our traditional markets in the United States and in the United Kingdom.
In the United Kingdom our soft lumber has to compete with the products of the Soviet block and the Scandinavian countries. Besides having to compete in Europe against trade areas such as the common market, the outer seven, the Soviet bloc and others which are developing over there, in order to remove tariff barriers within their territories where services, labour and capital will be able to move as if there were no international boundaries, it is to be expected that tariff barriers will be set up against the countries which are not part of the areas concerned.
Mr. Chairman, in order to show the importance of our forest product exports, I shall quote figures given to me by the forestry division of the dominion bureau of statistics.
In 1959, we exported to Great Britain 671,-
359,000	f.b.m. of timber, or a total value of $53,052,264. In the same year, we exported to the United States 3,485,512,000 f.b.m. of timber, or a total value of $259,581,652. For the same year, our exports of plywood to the United Kingdom reached 1,517,000 f.b.m., valued at $41,337, while our exports to the United States reached 495,343,000 f.b.m., or $16,973,153.
Again in 1959, we exported to the United Kingdom 155,298,000 f.b.m. of plywood, averaging three quarters of an inch thick, for a value of $10,476,336. During the same year, we exported 28,814,000 f.b.m. of plywood of a total value of $4,596,826 to the U.S.

Mr. Chairman, as far as our domestic markets and the sales of our soft and hardwood species are concerned, it is a well known fact that when construction is up, so is the demand for our wood products. But as family housing construction declined last year, our lumber producers were also affected.
At this point of my remarks, and in relation with the competition on the lumber market, I should like to quote an excerpt from the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects:
To assume that the marketing of Canadian forest products will present no serious problem would be naive.
Then there is also the possibility that the manufacture of newsprint and other pulps from alternative materials will become an economic reality: that potential markets in a number of relatively underdeveloped countries will be shut off by the erection there of newsprint mills based on extensive local resources such as bagasse (sugar-cane waste) or tropical hardwoods-
But the most disconcerting question mark of all has to do with the possible competition of countries behind the iron curtain and especially Russia whose forest resources are tremendous.
Mr. Chairman, I see on pages 225 and 226 of the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1962, that the number of civil servants in the administrative branch of the Department of Forestry has increased from 110 in 1960-61 to 188 in 1961-62. I should hope that French speaking or bilingual employees are in adequate number to give satisfaction and justice to the thousands of French speaking Canadians engaged in the production of forest products in Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, in March 1961, the Minister of Forestry announced the appointment of the following senior officials in his department: Mr. H. W. Beall, Ottawa, executive director of the new department; Mr. J. H. Jenkins, Vancouver, director of research on forest products; Mr. D. R. Redmond, Upper Musquodoboit, N.S., director of forestry research and Mr. M. L. Prebble, Saint John, N.B., director of forest entomology and pathology.
I should like to quote a few excerpts from an editoral written by Mr. Jean Taillefer, parliamentary reporter of Le Droit, under the title: "A matter of efficiency". This article appeared in Le Droit of March 13, 1961. I quote:
It is to be noted, though, that no one from Quebec has been appointed to any of the higher
positions.
The lack of Quebec representation is all the more surprising since forestry is one of the main industries of that province. It ranks second on a national scale, having 88.000 square miles of developed forest land. Only Ontario, with 101,000 square miles has more forest land than Quebec. Can we, therefore, believe that Quebec has no experts in that field?

Why is it so important to have bilingual personnel? For a very simple reason, which has nothing to do with emotionalism-efficiency.
Mr. Chairman, it should not be forgotten that the province of Quebec has a great number of French speaking forest producers, operating on a medium or a small scale, and I hope that the minister will see to it that somebody from Quebec is appointed when other important appointments are made in his department.

Mr. Chairman, I was very pleased to note the increase in forestry over the last year, which coincides with the time that the new minister has been in office. We from the maritime area were very proud to see a member from our area take the portfolio of forestry. We recognize that in the minister who now holds that post we have a man who knows the forest industry and is very interested in the development of what is one of our most important Atlantic industries.
I have before me an article in the Cape Breton Post of Friday December 30, 1960, referring to a speech by Mr. R. M. Fowler, the president of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association and the newsprint association of Canada. In the article Mr. Fowler is reported as having said that 1960 was a very good year in forestry and his figures showed an increase of 5 per cent in the output of the Canadian pulp and paper industry last year. Mr. Fowler also pointed out that newsprint production in 1960 was a record at about
6,735,000	tons, 4 per cent above the previous high of 1956. Quoting Mr. Fowler, the article goes on to say:
This increase was the largest shown in any of the last 13 years and was more than the modest amount of new productive capacity which became available in Canada during the year. As a result, newsprint operating ratios averaged about 88.5 per cent compared with 85 per cent of a smaller capacity in 1959.
He also went on to ooint out that shipments overseas were almost 20 per cent higher than in 1959, with increases to the United Kingdom, Australia and South America being particularly large. Speaking ot tne future he said that he expected to see substantial increases in the markets for Canadian newsprint and paper products generally.
The matter of forestry is very important to me because in my riding at the present time there is being constructed a pulp mill which will have a marked effect upon the province of Nova Scotia in the years ahead. In 1959, at the invitation of the government of Nova Scotia and with the assistance provided by the government, Stora Kopperberg

Supply-Forestry
of Sweden and the Scott Paper people of the United States combined to form Nova Scotia Pulp Limited and began construction of a $40 million mill. The target date for the operation of the mill is January, 1962. The mill will produce 250 tons per day and 125,000 tons a year of high grade pulp. It will utilize
250,000	cords a year of eight-foot pulpwood sticks, almost 800 cords a day and at peak times some 2,000 cords a day. If this pulp-wood were stacked in a continuous four-foot pile, it would be some 380 miles long. It would extend from Cape North in Inverness county to Yarmouth at the other end of the province. Most of the wood, it is estimated, will come from the seven eastern counties of Nova Scotia where there are some 3.3 million acres of productive forest land. About 1 million of these acres are owned by the crown in the right of the province and the balance is privately owned.
One of the reasons the provincial government was so interested in bringing Stora Kop-perberg into the province was that this firm had been, for many years, operating in Sweden and had learned there the most modern and best ways of forest management. Under its contract with the province, it will set up a proper forest management operation on the crown lands and will assist private woodlot owners in every way possible to farm their wood lands in the most productive manner in terms of the pulp which will be needed in the years ahead. Under the plan divisional foresters will be set up at New Glasgow, Port Hawkesbury and Baddeck.
The impact of this new mill upon the economy of the province can be illustrated by the fact that the pulp cut in Nova Scotia in 1958 was some 270,874 cords, and in 1959 was 288,029 cords. If we add to this the 250,000 cords that will be required by Nova Scotia Pulp Limited each year, it will be seen that the new mill will almost double the demand for pulpwood in the province of Nova Scotia. It has been estimated that the new money involved, in the hands of the people cutting pulp alone, will be in excess of some $10 million a year. In addition to the new market which has been developed this way in eastern Nova Scotia, over the last year we have seen a very marked increase in the demand for pulpwood for export. New markets have opened up in Europe, particularly in western Germany and shipments are being made now from Louisburg and it is proposed there will be some from Whycocomagh in Inverness county. I have before the Minister of Public Works now proposals to provide special wharfage facilities at Whycocomagh, Louisburg and Port Hastings to facilitate the shipment of this pulp. I hope that something can
[Mr. MacLellan.l
be provided at these centres as soon as possible to assist this rapidly growing industry.
I notice that all members when speaking on the estimates of this department referred to the necessity, in terms of the future of Canada, of forest management plans which will provide for the very substantial need for forest products in the future. There was a time when Canada could afford to waste its forest products, but that time has now gone. We must look forward in the years ahead to ensuring that we have a sufficient cut to meet the new markets and the new demands which are opening up. Apropos of that, Mr. Chairman, I would point out that in the province of Nova Scotia, more than in any other province, this is a particularly important question. I spoke a moment ago of the large market for pulpwood there will be in the province after January, 1962.
It is interesting to note that Nova Scotia has a rather small productive forested land compared with other provinces. Nova Scotia has some 9,668,000 acres of productive forested land. Our neighbours in New Brunswick have some 15,237,000 acres. Nova Scotia has less than 10 per cent of the forested land of Quebec where there is over 140 million acres of productive forested land. The province of Ontario has some 106 million acres of forested land. It will be seen that the necessity for forest management and the preservation of our forests, is much more important and urgent in Nova Scotia than in any other part of Canada because in our province trees are scarcer than elsewhere in relation to the demand that is now developing for pulpwood and for forest products in general. In Nova Scotia every tree must be properly utilized in the years ahead.
However, Mr. Chairman, the difficulties of forest management in Nova Scotia are greater than they are in the other provinces. In Nova Scotia, there is a relatively small part of the forested area which is owned by the crown. About 20 per cent of the forested area in Nova Scotia is crown land. This can be contrasted with about 50 per cent crown ownership in New Brunswick and some 90 per cent in the province of Quebec. The putting into operation of plans for forest management and tree farming is much easier, of course, in provinces where large acreages are owned by the crown and arrangements can easily be made for the development of publicly owned land. The job is much more difficult where, as in Nova Scotia, the task is to bring to the attention of private wood-lot owners how important modern woodlot management is for immediate use and for the preservation of our forests for the future. This is a very difficult problem which will

have to be worked out between the province and the woodlot owners. However, we will have the leadership of Nova Scotia Pulp Limited in solving this problem, and they have some of the best experts in the world in the field of forest management.
I was very pleased, Mr. Chairman, to see the quick way in which the new Department of Forestry, under this new minister, has responded to the need for the development of better forestry practices in Canada, and has generally stimulated the forest industry. The program whereby this government pays 50 per cent of the cost of access roads to be built into timberlands will be particularly helpful in Nova Scotia. I understand that under the program now in effect some 130 miles of boundary line in Inverness county will be cleaned out, some 90 miles in Richmond county, about 90 miles in Cape Breton county and similar mileages in other counties in eastern Nova Scotia. This will facilitate forest management, the preservation of the forest in case of forest fire, and generally give access to the timberlands for the development of better timber operations. While fire is a very dangerous thing in any part of Canada, it is particularly to be feared in Nova Scotia where our forests are so small in relation to the market that is to be developed in the province. I note that 50 per cent of the cost of the equipment for fire protection is now provided by the Department of Forestry. I hope that close liaison will continue between the department of lands and forests in Nova Scotia and the federal Department of Forestry in providing better forest protection in the province of Nova Scotia. The department of lands and forests under the able administration of the Hon. E. Haliburton in Nova Scotia, has a big job ahead in the organizational work which must be done to help the woodlot owners provide the pulpwood for the new mill. As I have said, it represents a doubling of last year's pulpwood cut.
The province will have to initiate an extensive project of education among the private woodlot owners. I think this should be in two forms. There should certainly be adult education among the farmers who own woodlots now directed toward efficient wood-lot management and there should be education in the schools so that our young people will learn proper forest management techniques. Above all, our young people should learn to appreciate the need for proper forest management in the province. I was very pleased to note the special grant that has been provided by the Department of Forestry for emergency work in Cape Breton Island in the months immediately ahead, when extra
Supply-Forestry
work will be needed because of the unfortunate mine closings. The money set aside to be used along with the contributions of the department of lands and forests in Nova Scotia will certainly give a big impetus to the work that the provinces must do in establishing a satisfactory forestry corps, in providing trees that can be planted on privately owned lands and otherwise in the development of woodlot management practice.
I know it is not within the authority of the federal department to originate very much in a direct way in forestry management practices as this is a matter under the authority and aegis of the province. However, I should like to see the minister do everything he can to assist Nova Scotia in the big job that is ahead in the establishment of illustration stations to teach forest management methods in woodland replanting and so on. Certainly as I watch this new industry mushrooming in the province and realize what a great boom it will give to all of eastern Nova Scotia, it is with particular pleasure that I see as head of the federal Department of Forestry such a good friend of Nova Scotia and such a well known, warmly liked and respected leader from the maritime provinces.

speechtext:
I hope the minister this afternoon, in introducing his estimates for the first time in this new department, will take into consideration some of the officials he has in the gallery and see to it that they are rewarded for having to be here on July 1 which normally should be a holiday for them.
I also hope the minister will take into consideration some of the remarks that have been made, particularly those by such veteran foresters as the hon. member for Kootenay West who is probably one of the only members of the committee who is completely familiar with modernization in the forest industry, controlling and operating as he does a large tract of forest that is not subject to any of the abuses that occur in my area. He has told me on a number of occasions that his land will now produce more lumber than it did when he first started to operate that forest. That certainly is not the situation in my part of the country. This is one of the reasons why I am so pleased that this ministry has been set up and why I suggest that consideration should be given to that type of forest control.
I was very much surprised a few years ago to find that a company with which I was negotiating on behalf of their workers informed me that they expected to be out of that area in five years. The reason I was surprised was that this operation had been continuing under the same company for

Supply-Forestry
something over 40 years. It seemed to me that if they had cut that long ago on their first limit, they would soon be ready to go back and to start recutting the area which they had previously cut over. I think this was a legitimate hope, and the hope that most Canadians have, namely that our forest industry, because it is renewable, has renewed itself and that we have as much forest today as we had many years ago.
In this case the manager had practised many of the best forms of forest culture without going into such things as assisting nature in reforestation which many of these operators have said is of no value. However, he informed me that it will be at least 90 years before they will be able to make any economical cut of lumber off the first limits this company went over. This seems to me to be something which should be of immediate importance to the department and about which they should try to do something right away.
We have listened many times to those who are interested in silviculture tell us that the forest will regenerate in those areas where reforestation has taken place, that reforestation is a natural thing and that there is not any necessity to help nature along. For those who say this and who think this, may I say that all they have to do is to look a few miles from the city of Ottawa or up the Ottawa valley. They may be surprised to find what has happened to the white pine industry that years ago gave this region such security when it was thought this forest would be perpetual. They only have to look up the Ottawa valley now and note the very limited forests and stands of white pine.
It is quite true that in my area of northern Ontario red pine and jack pine will have a certain amount of regeneration themselves. But because this is a renewable resource, because it is one of the resources that we have and can leave to our children, it behooves us not only to leave it in as good shape as we received it but to leave it in much better shape, and to give consideration to the needs that are already apparent and will become increasingly apparent as the years go by.
This means, of course, that we must concentrate on conservation, and that we must use some of the other resources. We must look to the maintaining and conserving of our water and water resources or we are not going to be able to reforest many of these areas which the Minister of Agriculture now hopes will be brought under an agricultural program for reforestation. If we do not practise conservation in some of the allied fields, this is not going to be possible and we are going to find that the land which has been

cut over-and quite a bit of it in northern Ontario is now completely barren-will grow only scrub forest products for many years to come and that it will be another generation or two before anything of any value is produced in those areas.
I know of one small area where the timber was burnt over and jack pine came up. One of the sad parts of the situation is this. Those interested in silviculture would say that so many seeds germinated in that area and so many live trees were produced per square foot or per square yard whatever they measure it by; and while this was true, those trees reached a height of only 10 feet or 12 feet. They were a very poor type of tree. Fire got into them and they were burnt to the ground. In five or six years they came up again. By this time the trees that had burnt and fallen as a result of the previous fire, again caught fire. This is the sort of thing that has been going on. It has happened three or four times in my lifetime. There is nothing growing in that particular area and it has produced absolutely nothing.
This department has many facets, in my opinion. It has many opportunities to do a great deal of good for Canada and for the Canadian people, and the least of them is not the tourist industry. Of course, the problem we are going to have with a federal forestry department is that it is competing with terrifically rich provincial counterparts. The one in Ontario is probably the most expensive department we have. It is a department that does not take in enough money to pay for its expenditures. It is a particular department that has all types of public facilities for spreading its doctrine or its information. Its educational field is almost unlimited. The federal government is, without doubt, going to have trouble in co-ordinating some of the activities of these departments. One of them would be the problem with the tourist industry. It has been maintained by bush operators that if you allow the tourists in, of course, they will create terrific fire hazards and the limits will suffer as a result of tourist travelling through the bush. However, we have in Ontario, I am sure, been able to solve this to a great extent by having fire ratings, and I am pleased to note that the federal government is now co-ordinating these fire services and fire protection services through the forest research division.
We have found that if you post a rating to the tourist industry and the rating remains medium, the difficulties, for which it does not follow the tourists are responsible, seem to be eliminated to an extent. The travelling of the tourist population through the forests does as much good as it does harm, in my

opinion, because the tourists then see the advantages of forest control, the need for reforestation and the need for roads and other facilities. I hope to live to see the day when many of these areas which are now well cut over, and particularly those which are not, but which are in the process of being cut, may be driven into by car. I hope to see the day when we shall And permanent residences in the forests, and permanent towns, and when the forests will be managed in such a way that we shall have a sustained yield in perpetuity. This can be done, and it has been done in other countries. There is no reason why we should not begin at once working towards perpetuity in the yield of our forest products.
This involves more than the maintenance of the forests. It may be necessary to change the type of tree which we have produced, as has been necessary in the United States. It may be that in a few years we shall have to plant trees of the type they have been planting in some of the southern states and these can be adapted to our climate. Many of these trees can be used in the production of pulp and paper. They have short life span. They will produce much faster than the trees we now use. It is true they produce an inferior grade of paper, but the advantage of the rapid growth and the rapid production of these trees may make it necessary for the department to be aware of their potential and the adaptability of these trees to our area.
There is another field which affects us in northern Ontario and that is in relation to the utilization of forest products. Our white pine industry has had between a 60 per cent and 65 per cent utilization of its products. In other countries it is reported that the utilization sometimes goes up as high as 100 per cent or 98 per cent. They even utilize the leaves, in some cases, they tell me, and put them to some use. In northern Ontario in recent years we have been able to take advantage of developments that are taking place in countries such as Sweden. Some of our manufacturers have gone to Sweden and to Germany and have been able to buy equipment in those countries and learn the knowhow necessary to operate plants, and they are now producing a number of varieties of wood products which are not in competition with the lumber industry. Abitibi is to be congratulated on this, particularly on the development of their chip board plant at Sturgeon Falls. The Jamar Plywood company at Sturgeon Falls has been using poplar wood for making veneer. They are now using a birch veneer face and producing an exceptionally nice type of plywood which is readily saleable at reasonable prices. In previous years in areas that were cut over either the birch
Supply-Forestry
was cut and left on the ground or it was not cut at all, and many of the old trees, when the spruce and pine were cut down, died because the protection was taken away from them. Those trees that are now useable are being used for this type of veneer. This has produced a whole new industry and provided employment for a great number of employees who could not be employed in the only other industry, that of mining. So, if the government is watching these developments, as are many in the lumbermen's association, the Ontario provincial forestry department and other associations, I am quite sure processes can be developed which will lead to a much greater utilization of our forest resources. This would, of course, also assist in developing and promoting new industries and new types of products such as we have seen develop in the last few years.
I do not know how much work the federal government has done in the past in relation to some of these projects. I was interested in the process which A. J. McFadden were using of taking very short step lumber from their white pine mill, short pieces which would otherwise be useless because of their size, cutting out anything which was of no use and putting them together by an electronic glue process, producing a board four by eight or four by 12 or four by 16. This produced an acceptable product, one suitable for a number of uses. They immediately ran into the problem of maintaining the same moisture content on one side of the board as on the other. It was used for external purposes. The government, it seems to me, could have given them a great deal of assistance at first if they had been active in this particular field.
The federal government, also through the forestry branch, could give more assistance than has been available to the lumber industry in the marketing of lumber products. In eastern Canada, in eastern Ontario, we have been plagued in recent years by the fact that traditional markets in the United States and Asia were lost, in the main, to the west coast. They were immediately in competition with producers in eastern Canada. It appears to me that the federal government, through their own department, in this way will be able to assess much better than it has in the past the necessity of developing a market in China and in the other countries of Asia for the lumber that is produced on the west coast. This lumber, if it is dumped out of its traditional markets into eastern Canada, will seriously affect the prices both of eastern and western lumber.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre referred to fire control. This has become one of the greatest blights of the forest industry.

Supply-Forestry
It is one that can eliminate a complete limit, so that a company almost overnight loses its means of survival. Weather, electrical storms, factors over which man has no control at all are playing a great role in this field. I was interested in the hon. member's suggestion that we should use more aircraft, and that we should bring this activity under federal control. I hope the hon. member is right, but I should be very surprised if the federal government is in any position to do anything about fire control in the provincial field unless it be through an increase in the contributions to the provinces in this particular field. It seems to me that fires can be fought only by people on the ground. If these individuals are not placed at the scene of the fire as quickly as possible the fire gets out of control and very little can be done about it at that stage.
I recommend to the government that rather than going into a program of buying aircraft to be used in a national fire protection service, it should increase its appropriations to the provinces, assisting them to continue the work now being done. In my opinion most of the provinces, although I can really only speak for the two, in regard to which I have made observations, are doing a great deal in this field and have proven capable of carrying on, unless of course a province is hit by a disaster such as appears to have hit the province of Newfoundland. The fire prevention techniques used there have had little effect. People there are being accused of setting the fires deliberately for the purpose of creating work. Similar accusations have been made in respect of the province of Ontario, as well as other provinces.
I think this area of fighting forest fires is one in which the federal government should make more contributions. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre when he suggests army personnel should be used wherever possible and when the necessity arises, but I suggest the army is not the best agency in this regard. While the army contains a readily available force and its personnel are capable of taking orders and doing the job, which is not the case very often in respect to men who are commandeered in areas to fight fires, it is not the most effective agency which could be used. Incidentally, among the individuals commandeered to fight fires in specific areas are included white collar workers and the like who are not accustomed to using shovels and the other tools, such as pumps, used to fight fires, and do not make good fire fighters even in cases of emergency. I do agree that army personnel should be used but suggest, however, that the major contribution this government could

make toward fire fighting lies in the field of research and the provision of assistance to the provinces.
One of the last subjects to which I wish to refer has relation to a government agency such as the industrial development bank through which financial assistance can be given to companies not in a position to expend the necessary amounts of money for the installation of efficient fire fighting equipment. Many mills now operating in the province of Ontario are poorly equipped in this regard, and perhaps not sufficiently informed as to the proper use of the equipment they have so as to make full use of it, or the equipment which they might acquire if funds were made available for that purpose.
This department can give assistance to these companies in two ways. First, by conducting a survey regarding the anticipated yield over the next few years which these different mills should enjoy. In other words, the department should help these companies assess their anticipated yields and instruct them in the efficient and advantageous operation of their mills in this regard.
For example, in northern Ontario there are a number of portable mills in operation. They are usually put in on a limited cut basis and under normal circumstances take only the cream of the crop leaving the rest standing in the area. As a result it is not advantageous for anyone else to come in and service the limit as I believe it should be serviced. It might be much more advantageous to these companies to put in mills even smaller than portable mills. The portable mills now in use are portable only in the sense that they can be moved with a great deal of effort by truck, but some of them in my area cut up to 100,000 feet per day. I am sure the minister will agree that type of mill is not portable in the normal sense.
The modernization program which I have suggested can be undertaken only if the companies involved are provided with new sources of money. I suggest that in many cases they do not possess the necessary information to convince the officials of the industrial development bank that their operations are such to warrant the lending of the amount of money required.
They are not in possession of that type of information only because they have neglected to hire accountants and agents to provide them with it. Officials of this department or other experts are much more able to assess the situation and make recommendations which, if followed, could possibly lead to the continuation of a successful industry upon which communities have depended for many years.

I hope the minister in closing the debate will indicate that he is receiving co-operation from provincial governments in the implementation of this necessarily continuous program in an attempt to perpetuate the yield from this type of operation so that those industries which have failed in the past years can be rejuvenated and put back into production with resultant benefit to the communities which have depended upon them for their livelihood.

Mr. Chairman, I regret very much that I have to rise on a question of privilege in connection with certain remarks made by the hon. member for Timiskaming in referring to the member for Kootenay West. In view of that hon. member's kindly and glowing references to my forestry activities I should not like the impression created that I am in any sense of the word a capitalist, because I am a socialist.
Oh, oh.
I am a socialist who looks upon himself as a trustee for the nation until the advent of democratic socialism.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question. Would the description feudal lord be a little more appropriate?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I did not intend that my remarks be construed to mean that anyone connected with the forest industry was a capitalist. I should think anyone interested in that field would be well aware of the fact that most socialistic countries manage their forests in a very efficient manner. I believe the hon. member for Kootenay West is advocating a program followed by most socialist countries-Sweden is a good example-of up to date, advantageous and efficient forestry control.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot compete with the hon. member for Kootenay West either as a member of the feudal class or as a socialist, because my connection with the forest industry was quite a long time ago and highly proletarian. I worked in a box factory once at Norwood for 20 cents per hour.
Oh, oh.
And subsequently spent a summer timber cruising at $35 per month.
You were overpaid.

That was quite a long time ago when the dollar stretched much further than it does at the present time.
I did not intend to speak on this subject but am prompted to do so after listening to
Supply-Forestry
the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, because I want to reinforce an excellent point he made. Before doing that I should like to say a word or two about an observation made by the hon. member for Timiskaming.
It so happens, as every hon. member of this house knows, that there have been very serious fires in my constituency which actually destroyed some of the houses in one of the settlements and threatened the total existence of a great many others. Happily the rain we had there two or three days ago seems to have removed the threat. Unless there is a good deal more rain-and there has been vei'y little in Newfoundland since a year ago this spring-that threat is bound to persist.
The appeal made by the hon. member for Timiskaming, and possibly by other hon. members when I was not in the chamber is one in which I should like to join heartily. I believe that anything the new Department of Forestry can do to aid in research into more effective methods of fighting fires will be one of the most productive expenditures of public money that can possibly be made in this country because it still happens, notwithstanding our great mineral wealth and all the other resources of this country, that the two greatest crops we grow in Canada are trees and grain; and if we look after our basic soil and our basic resources we can continue to grow them for all time. It seems that this year, because of weather conditions, both of them are seriously threatened. We know that millions and millions of dollars of public funds have been expended over the years in research into the various aspects of the wheat industry, and we know that all that has been spent has been more than repaid many times over in additional returns not merely to the farmers but to the whole Canadian economy. The forest industry is, I suppose, today the biggest single source of income to the Canadian people as a whole if we look at all of its ramifications. It is indeed fitting that at this time we should be recognizing that fact by having a separate department of government, though we all recognize that the jurisdiction that belongs to this department as compared with the jurisdiction of the provinces is very limited indeed. For my part I am not going to expect the minister to work miracles. He, of course has a very real personal knowledge -a lifetime knowledge-of the forest industry himself, and though I do not agree with his politics, I find him an agreeable person. Although I do not expect miracles, I am sure he is going to bring that practical experience to the administration of his department and mix it with the scientific knowledge that already exists and the great

Supply-Forestry
scientific knowledge that we hope will be developed in the years to come.
I am not going to make a general discourse about the industry. What I rose to do was to speak about two things: One was this fire situation which in the province of Newfoundland-and apparently in some of the other provinces as well because there have been very serious fires in northern Ontario, in Manitoba, and in British Columbia-is serious indeed. We do know that these forest fires do not destroy the timber; at least they do not always destroy it or they do not generally destroy it. We also know that the greatest possible care has to be taken to harvest that timber at the right time after there has been a fire, and sometimes exceptional measures must be taken to do that. I am speaking now particularly of Newfoundland. I admit that this will primarily be a problem for the provincial government and for the two paper companies and the other interests that have title or leases. The situation will vary in each particular case. I plead with the department to give, as I am sure they can and intend to, every possible co-operation to the government of Newfoundland and to the government of any other province that needs it in ensuring that the burnt timber will be harvested at the right time and in the most effective way so that we can minimize to the greatest degree possible this very serious loss that there is going to be in any event. No one in the circumstances we have had in this last little while could have done more than was done.
In this context, sir, perhaps you would permit me to say that I think everyone in the area concerned appreciated enormously the ready co-operation of the armed forces of Canada, of the armed forces of the United States which were most helpful in the area, and also the generous and unsolicited co-operation extended by the government of the province of Quebec, the only province which really has a common boundary with the province of Newfoundland and which has a great deal of effective fire fighting equipment, some of which was made available. As the member for the district in which those fires took place I should like to say that this help from the government of Canada, the government of the United States and the government of Quebec was deeply appreciated by the people and will not be forgotten.
I rose also to say a word or two about the subject mentioned by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. He pointed out that in addition to this new mill in Cape Breton there was also developing in Europe a market for pulpwood, and that is true. He appealed to the minister, though, of course, it is not directly this minister's responsibility, to offer

his support to any steps that might be required to provide shipping facilities for that pulpwood. Actually the minister-and I am glad he is in the house and can hear me- who would have to provide those facilities is the Minister of Public Works. But this minister has not the same intimate relationship, either officially or in his past experience of forestry, that the Minister of Forestry has, and I am sure he will be the first to admit it. But there is not any question whatsoever that all over eastern Canada-and I am sure the Minister of Forestry knows this also- there is a great deal of over-mature timber which the pulp and paper companies have not been able to absorb because it was not as conveniently situated or for some other reason, and which should be cut as quickly as possible or it is going not merely to perish itself but do harm to the forest because if over-mature timber is allowed to stand and then to fall I am told it is a much greater prey to disease than is young healthy timber. This is of the utmost importance.
I admit that in the management of those forests the provinces and the companies concerned have the prime responsibility. But particularly in some of the provinces which are anxious to have federal co-operation there is a great deal that a wise federal department can do to help. I thing I can say, although I am not in any way authorized to speak for the provincial authority, that in Newfoundland there will be a ready welcome for any assistance that the minister and his department are able to offer in this respect.
I should like to say also, sir, just as I said to the Minister of Public Works the other day when his estimates were before the house-I think it bears repetition because the point is exactly that which the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond was seeking to make as well-it so happens that a wharf had to be replaced in the northern part of my riding because it had been there for many years and it had rotted away. It was going to cost a very large sum of money. I confess when the project came before me as a member of the previous government I gasped a little at the amount in relation to the size of the place and wondered whether it was really going to return-not to the treasury, because those wharves do not return perhaps very much to the treasury, but to the economy-an amount commensurate with the cost. A wharf was built by the present government at a place called Carman-ville and millions of cords of pulpwood that no one had any idea were going to be cut and shipped over that wharf are being shipped over it to Italy at this very moment and a good price is being received. This is wood

that is surplus to the requirements of either the companies in Newfoundland. It is wood that is mostly over-mature and that would be a dead loss to the Canadian economy if it were not cut. In that whole strait shore area of my constituency it has kept dozens of men and their families off unemployment insurance and off relief in the past winter.
There is another area in my riding called Goose bay, not the Goose Bay in Labrador but Goose bay on the island of Newfoundland, where a similar operation is about to commence. In this particular area around a settlement called Lethbridge, not that more recent place in Alberta which is perhaps somewhat better known but the original Lethbridge, there is a great deal of timber that should also be cut and salvaged before it becomes over-mature. A useful industry can be developed there that will do for that area what has been done by the development at Carmanville, but a wharf somewhere in that bay is going to be needed in order to make it possible to ship that timber economically.
I know this is not the minister's responsibility, but I am suggesting to him that he give his colleague, the Minister of Public Works, a nudge every once in a while to find out whether that minister's engineers are really working hard enough at this project and getting ahead with it. It is for that reason that I rose to speak. I am often labelled in this house as a free trader, but I know that we would all rather have our pulpwood wholly processed in Canada instead of shipping it as pulpwood, but the minister knows and I know that if we have not got the plant to do it and we have over-mature wood for which there is a cash market we are crazy not to take it.
With the great prosperity that has developed in Europe as a result of the common market and with the vastly increased market there, there is a chance for us in eastern Canada to have a good cash crop, such as the wheat crop has been in the past to the west, that will help to tide us over until the time when we can get processing plants in eastern Canada to process all the wood there. The fact that this wood is being produced and that means are being found to produce it and ship it would encourage people to come in there with capital and build processing plants. I suggest that any and every kind of encouragement that the Minister of Forestry gives, both within the cabinet and with the provincial governments of the eastern provinces, particularly the province of Newfoundland, will be very welcome indeed and will, I am sure, bring a great return to the Canadian economy.

May I ask the hon. member a question? Does the province of Newfoundland permit the export of wood cut on crown lands?

It is permitted but under very strict control as, of course, there should be. We do not want young growing timber exported before its time, but in Newfoundland, as I am sure is the case in practically all the other provinces, there is the most rigorous kind of forest management applied, and I would not advocate anything else.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks at this time will be rather brief. I should like to extend my congratulations and best wishes to the minister on his assumption of this highly important portfolio. In the Niagara peninsula we do not have any forests and we have very few woodlots. However, we have eight paper mills, some of which are very large, and the supply of pulpwood is most important to us. It comes in by boat and it also comes in by rail.
A great deal has been said today about pulpwood so I will not deal with that matter but I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the scarcity of hardwood which is becoming acute in the province of Ontario. Just recently the seaway authority had reason to purchase substantial quantities of oak timbers and they were just not to be found in this country. As a result, on three occasions large orders for oak timbers had to go to the United States.
I bring to the attention of the minister the need to take action as to this problem. I am thinking in terms of trees such as oak, ash, beech and hickory which used to grow extensively in the province of Ontario but at the present time seem to be almost dying out. There are other kinds of valuable trees such as the sycamore, plane tree, basswood and hard chestnut which are almost things of the past. I feel that attention should be given to trying to bring trees of this type into production again.
I should also like to refer to our shade trees. Too often we see trees planted along city streets and around houses that are just not suitable from the point of view of growing and becoming proper shade trees. When one visits some of the old estates in Ontario one will see beautiful trees growing there of types that are almost extinct in other parts of the country.
In conjunction with the department of lands and forests of the province I believe the minister should give consideration to the three points I have mentioned, the scarcity of hardwood timber in the province of Ontario, the scarcity of special trees such as basswood, chestnut and walnut, which

Supply-Forestry
used to grow in great profusion and are now almost a thing of the past, and the matter of shade trees because they too are not receiving the attention that they should. Varieties that are most suitable for planting are sometimes hard to get.

My only wish is, that Canada's unemployed could find jobs as easily as the Minister of Forestry.
Unfortunately for him, his employment will not last very long, I am afraid, since following the next general election, he will have to be satisfied, if he is not defeated, with being a private member.

I should like the minister to tell the house what amounts were paid New Brunswick for insect control, and how much Quebec received from Ottawa in that connection, because in the years past that pest plagued Quebec forests and my impression is that the cost of the air spraying done then was borne exclusively by the private companies and by the province of Quebec.

Therefore, I should appreciate it to learn from the Minister of Forestry what are the amounts received by the province of Quebec through joint agreements on assistance to light disease due to insects or cutworm.
I take this opportunity to wish him once more every success in his department. Like the other speakers who preceded me, I deplore the fact that he did not give French Canadians a fair share of higher positions, especially when the Quebec forest industry ranks among the most important in this country. speechtext: I believe all Ontario members probably received the letter from the Ontario forestry association in which they point out the terms of reference of the department itself. They ask that the annual grant of $20,000 be increased to $100,000. I will not go into the particulars, but they point out that the Ontario government contributes $10,000. They also point out that their total budget is something over $1 million annually, that the members donate $472,000 and that the federal government contribution at the present time amounts to only 4 per cent of the total. They have requested that this grant be increased to $100,000. Has the minister given consideration to this request from the Ontario forestry association? If so, is there contemplation of supplementing this grant through supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member for Timiskaming I would say that in the estimates for the fiscal year-not the current one but the next one-the department is giving very careful consideration to the request of the Canadian forestry association. It is not contemplated that there will be any additional item except the $20,000 during the current year.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: May I ask the leader of the house to be more gentle with me than with some of my colleagues and tell me the business of the house for next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: A courteous question requires a courteous reply. I am happy to inform the hon. member that on Monday we shall begin with Bill No. C-92 which has to do with the Criminal Code and consider an amendment suggested by the Senate. The second item would be the bill to amend the Excise Act.
The Excise Tax Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. I am addressing my remarks to the hon. member for St. Denis. The Excise Act. The third item would be the bill to amend the Excise Tax Act. The next would be the bill to amend the Customs Tariff followed by the amendment to the Industrial Development Bank Act.
We shall have available on Monday the resolution with regard to the Canadian National Railway finances which, by consent,

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I doubt whether we shall be able to reach it on Monday.
Is it clear that on Tuesday we shall definitely take up, as the Minister said on Friday, the Bank of Canada Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is correct. On Tuesday we shall deal with any unfinished items from Monday's order of business, for example, the C.N.R. financing bill if it passes the resolution stage. I presume the Income Tax Act would then become available, so it is obvious now it would be possible to complete the business next week.
I wish to make sure that the Bank of Canada Act will definitely come up on Tuesday. Is that clear?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is right.
